d: Gunfire directed along the length rather than the breadth of a formation
ety: Borrowed from French enfilade.
s: Uncle Charles, a truly unparalleled slinger of shit, is laying down an enfilade of same, trying to mollify men who seem way more in need of a good brow-mopping than I.

d: An artificial or inferior substitute or imitation
ety: Borrowed from German Ersatz (“replacement, substitute”), a back-formation from ersetzen (“to replace, to substitute”).
s: “You do Berlin a disservice, baron. We too have mastered a few things: ersatzes, for instance, and the metaphysics of fictionalism—”

d: A long flag; often tapering
ety: From Late Middle English pennon, penoun (“long narrow flag attached to a lance or used in other contexts; one who bears a pennon, knight bachelor; plume of feathers; strip around the edge of a shield”), from Anglo-Norman penun (“feather of an arrow”), penoun (“flag attached to a lance”), Middle French pennon, penoun, and Old French penon (“flag attached to a lance”) (modern French pennon), from pe
s: In 1821 the hobby-horse could have a real mane and a pretty topknot of wire, pennons and bells but with no wheels at the back.

d: Being of striking appropriateness and pertinence
ety: From Latin appositus, past participle of adponere, from ad- + ponere (“to put, place”). See apposition.
s: Or is that just the way art is now? The neo-Victorian craze is very apposite.

d: A nobleman of highest rank in Spain or Portugal
ety: Borrowed from Spanish grande (adjective), from Latin grandis (“large, great”). Doublet of grand and grande.
s: This Duke Ricardo, Señores, as you probably know, is a grandee from Spain whose lands are the best in Andalucía.

d: The intended meaning of a communication
ety: From Middle English purporten, from Anglo-Norman purporter and Old French porporter (“convey, contain, carry”), from pur-, from Latin pro (“forth”) + Old French porter (“carry”), from Latin portō (“carry”).
s: For she her sex under that strange purport / Did use to hide.

d: A characteristic language of a particular group (as among thieves)
ety: Borrowed from French patois (“regional dialect or language”), c. 1635.
s: In the patois of insurance, the winery will go bare into this year’s burning season, which experts predict to be especially fierce.

d: A book of prayers to be recited daily certain priests and members of religious orders
ety: From Latin breviārium (“summary”) (compare abbreviation), ultimately from brevis (“short”). Doublet of brevier and brimborion.
s: Sister took out her breviary and said her evening office.

d: A light long-handled racket used by badminton players
ety: From Middle English batildore, batylledore, batildure, batyldoure, batyndore, probably as a blend of Middle English betel (“bat, club”) and Old Occitan batedor (“beater, bat”).
s: There were nights when it seemed to me that our position could be stormed by twenty Boy Scouts armed with airguns, or twenty Girl Guides armed with battledores, for that matter.

d: Sailing barge used especially in East Anglia
ety: From Middle English whery (“small boat”), of obscure origin but cognate to French houari and Breton ouari, as well as Welsh chweri (“small boat”).
s: The river was astir early and late with barges, wherries, and craft of every description.

d: A reckless and unprincipled reprobate
ety: From scape (“(archaic) escape”) + grace (“grace of god”).
s: He is now laden with that superabundant energy which makes a fool of a man, and a scapegrace of a boy, and he wants to work it off.

d: A gullible simpleton more to be pitied than despised
ety: Borrowed from Yiddish שנוק (shnuk, “person easily imposed upon or cheated”).
s: He’s just a schnook. She’s obviously using him but he keeps coming back for more abuse.

d: The use of tricks to deceive someone (usually to extract money from them)
ety: From French chicanerie (“trickery”), from chicaner, from Middle French chicaner, borrowed from Middle Low German schicken, from Old Saxon *skikkian, from Proto-West Germanic *skikkijan (“to order, arrange”). Related to German schicken (“to send, ship”), Middle English skekken (“to send forth, issue”).
s: They do not always find manors, got by rapine or chicanery, insensibly to melt away, as the poets will have it; or that all gold glides, like thawing snow, from the thief’s hand that grasps it.

d: (used of certain religious orders) barefoot or wearing only sandals
ety: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin discalceātus (“barefoot”) + -ed, rendering French déchaussé. By surface analysis, dis- + calced.
s: Brother John is a member of the Discalced Carmelites.

d: A person serving no apparent function
ety: From Late Latin supernumerarius (“extra soldier added to a legion; supernumerary”), from super (“above; beyond”) + numerus (“number; collection, quantity”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives from nouns or numerals). The word is analysable as super- + numeral + -ary.
s: The judge was a supernumerary, helping the regular judges whenever there was a surplus amount of work.

d: The characteristic sounds made by a horse
ety: Imitative; from 1774.
s: 1713-1714, John Arbuthnot, Memoirs of Martin Scriblerus your modern musicians want art to defend their windows from common nickers

d: Marked by speed and efficiency
ety: From Middle English expedycius (“useful, fitting”), from Latin expedītus (“disengaged, ready, convenient, prompt; unfettered, unencumbered”), past participle of expediō.
s: Our coachman and horses are so extremely expeditious!—I believe we drive faster than anybody.

d: Cause to be more favorably inclined; gain the good will of
ety: Borrowed from Latin conciliātus, perfect passive participle of conciliō (“to unite”), from concilium (“council, meeting”).
s: `Surely, my father,' I answered courteously, feeling certain that I should do well to conciliate this ancient Mammon of Unrighteousness.

d: An act of scaling by the use of ladders (especially the walls of a fortification)
ety: Borrowed from French escalade, from Italian scalata, from scalare (“to climb”), from scala (“ladder”), from Latin scālae (“ladder”). Doublet of scalade.
s: An escalade was required for the warriors to attack the troops.

d: A novice learning the rudiments of some subject
ety: From Late Latin abecedarius (from the first four letters of the Latin alphabet + -arius). Equivalent to abecedary + -an. Compare abecedary.
s: An Abecedarian is any poem constrained by alphabetical order.

d: A new word formed by joining two others and combining their meanings
ety: From Middle French portemanteau (“coat stand”), from porte (“he carries”, third-person singular present indicative of porter (“to carry”)) + manteau (“coat”), literally “[that which] carries coat”. The lexical sense (sense 2) was first used figuratively by Lewis Carroll in Through the Looking-Glass (1871) to describe the words he coined in the poem “Jabberwocky”, based on the concept of two words
s: Well then, ‘mimsy’ is ‘flimsy and miserable’ (there’s another portmanteau for you).

d: A deliberately invalid argument displaying ingenuity in reasoning in the hope of deceiving someone
ety: From Middle English safistre, soffistre, sofystry, sophestrie, sophestry, sophestrye, sophistre, sophistri, sophistrie, sophistry, sophistrye, sophystrye, from Old French sofisterie, sophistrie and Medieval Latin sophistria, Anglo-Latin sophestria, from Latin sophista, from Ancient Greek σοφιστής (sophistḗs, “wise man”), from σοφίζω (sophízō, “to be wise”), from σοφός (sophós, “wise”), equivalent
s: And so, my head hitting have to be real, solid, and true, with no sophistry or fantasy about them.

d: An acute insufficiency
ety: First attested at least as early as the late 1300s, and appearing in Tyndale’s Pentateuch (1530) as well as the Coverdale Bible (1535). From Middle English derth, derthe, derþe, probably from Old English *dīerþ, *dīerþu, from Proto-West Germanic *diuriþu, from Proto-Germanic *diuriþō (“costliness, preciousness, honour”); corresponding to dear + -th (abstract nominal suffix). Cognate with Old Saxon
s: The dearth of A.I. chips has been exacerbated because Nvidia, a longtime provider of the chips, has a virtual lock on the market.

d: Bear the expenses of
ety: From Middle French desfrayer, French défrayer, from dé- + Old French fraier (“to spend”).
s: In order to help defray the substantial costs involved, they then raised revenue through taking advertisements.

d: Fraught with danger
ety: From Middle English parles, parlous, perlous, [and other forms], a contraction of perilous (“dangerous; dreadful, terrible; morally corrupt, sinful, wicked; inauspicious, unlucky”) (and thus a doublet of perilous), from Old French perilleus, perillos, perillous, perilluse, perilleuse, perilleux (“very dangerous, perilous”) (modern French périlleux), from Latin perīculōsus (“dangerous, hazardous, p
s: The situation became parlous when the weather made resupply impossible.

d: Nonsensical talk or writing
ety: From Middle English trompery, from Middle French tromperie (“deceit”).
s: In that case there is no need for me to write about the trumpery scandal by which I was the sufferer—the innocent sufferer, I positively assert.

d: Exacting especially about details
ety: University slang, probably from fine.
s: Charming, he said in a finical sweet voice, showing his white teeth and blinking his eyes pleasantly.

d: Righteousness as a consequence of being honorable and honest
ety: From Middle English rectitude, from Middle French rectitude, from Late Latin rectitūdō (“straightness, uprightness”), from Latin rectus (“straight”), perfect passive participle of regō (“regulate, guide”).
s: “Sit with her all night if we have to,” Syd affirms with strenuous rectitude.

d: A pressing or urgent situation
ety: From Middle French exigence, from Late Latin exigentia (“urgency”) (from exigēns + -ia), from exigere (“to demand”).
s: My business is with you, and you only. You should not have undertaken your office, unless prepared for its various exigencies.

d: Belonging to some prior time
ety: Borrowed from Latin quondam. Compare whilom.
s: For the sleeper on the couch was not Akeley at all, but my quondam guide Noyes.

d: A publisher’s emblem printed in a book (usually on the title page)
ety: Borrowed from Late Latin colophōn, from Ancient Greek κολοφών (kolophṓn, “peak or finishing touch”).
s: He comes to the creation of man, and makes him the Colophon, or conclusion of all things else.

d: Of hair color; pale yellowish to yellowish brown
ety: From Middle English flaxen, flexon, flexin, from Old English fleaxen (“of flax; flaxen”), equivalent to flax + -en (“made of”). Compare Dutch vlassen.
s: The couple and their children have flaxen hair.

d: Open to two or more interpretations; or of uncertain nature or significance; or (often) intended to mislead
ety: From Late Latin aequivocus + -al, from aequus + vocō. By surface analysis, equi- + vocal.
s: For the beauties of Shakespeare are not of so dim or equivocal a nature as to be visible only to learned eyes.

d: A loud resonant repeating noise
ety: Borrowed from Latin clangor.
s: H. G. Wells' stark short story "The Cone" tells of a man's macabre revenge worked out in the clangour of a great steel works and railway lines and sidings.

d: The intellectual productivity of a creative imagination
ety: From Latin fēcunditās (“fruitfulness, fertility”), from fēcundus, equivalent to fecund + -ity.
s: The soil spawned humanity, as it bred frogs in the Rains, and the gap of the sickness of one season was filled to overflowing by the fecundity of the next.

d: A timid man or boy considered childish or unassertive
ety: From Middle English milksop, mylk sop, mylke soppe, equivalent to milk + sop.
s: “That milksop of a creature pretend to be worthy of such a woman as Mrs. Pendennis,” broke out the Doctor: “where will impudence stop next!”

d: Plausible but false
ety: From Middle English speciose, specious, from Anglo-Norman specious, Middle French specieux, and their etymon Latin speciōsus (“good-looking”).
s: This idea that we must see through what we have started is specious, however good it may sound.

d: A rectangular block of hewn stone used for building purposes
ety: From Middle English assheler, acheler, etc., from forms of Old French esselier (“wooden support, traverse beam”), from Medieval Latin ascelāris and assellāris (equivalent to a diminutive of early forms of ais (“plank”)), variant of *axillāris (attested only after the Renaissance), from Latin axilla (“little plank”) + -āris (“-ary: forming adjectives”), from axis (“axle, plank”) + -illa (“-ella: fo
s: The building, in a plain Tudor Gothic style, has a central door in chamfered ashlar surround.

d: Lean and wrinkled by shrinkage as from age or illness
ety: From wizen + -ed. Inherited from Middle English wisenen, from Old English wisnian, weosnian, from Proto-Germanic *wisnōjaną. Cognate with Icelandic visna.
s: He was old, too, wizened with age, and the hair on his face was gray.

d: A medicine used to relieve pain
ety: From Middle English anodine, from Medieval Latin anōdynos (“stilling or relieving pain”), from Ancient Greek ἀνώδυνος (anṓdunos, “free from pain”), from ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ὀδύνη (odúnē, “pain”). Adjective sense “noncontentious” probably through French anodin (“harmless, trivial”), of same origin.
s: The air was heavy with the perfume of the flowers, and their beauty seemed to bring him an anodyne for his pain.
